title: Modulation of quantum geometry and its coupling to pseudo-electric field by dynamic strain

paper_content.abstract:
Two-dimensional materials are a fertile ground for exploring quantum geometric phenomena, with
Berry curvature and its first moment, the Berry curvature dipole, playing a central role in their
electronic response. These geometric properties influence electronic transport and result in the
anomalous and nonlinear Hall effects, and are typically controlled using static electric fields or
strain. However, the possibility of modulating quantum geometric quantities in real-time remains
unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the dynamic modulation of Berry curvature and its moments,
as well as the generation of a pseudo-electric field and their coupling. By placing heterostructures
on a membrane, we introduce oscillatory strain together with an in-plane AC electric field and
measure Hall signals that are modulated at linear combinations of the frequencies of strain and
electric field. We also present direct experimental and theoretical evidence for coupling between
pseudo-electric field and quantum geometry that results in an unusual dynamic strain-induced Hall
response. This approach opens up a new pathway for controlling quantum geometry on demand,
moving beyond conventional static perturbations. The coupling of pseudo-electric field with Berry
curvature provides a framework for external electric field-free anomalous Hall response and opens
new avenues for probing the topological properties.
paper_content.introduction:
Two-dimensional (2D) materials have emerged as an exciting platform in condensed matter physics
and material sciences, offering unique opportunities to study, tune, and probe fundamental quantum
phenomena. From graphene to transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDC) and onwards to moiré
superlattices, these atomically thin systems exhibit properties such as tunable band gaps [1, 2],
high carrier mobility, strong spin-orbit coupling [3], and pronounced excitonic effects, making them
ideal candidates for next-generation quantum devices. Among the various approaches to tailor
their properties, the application of mechanical strain stands out as a versatile and non-invasive
tool. Strain enables modification of band structures, valley polarization [4, 5], and induces phase
transitions [6, 7], thereby significantly altering the electronic and optical responses.

A particularly intriguing aspect of 2D materials is the role of quantum geometry in governing
their physical responses [8], mainly encoded by Berry curvature and the Berry curvature dipole
(BCD) [9–11]. Berry curvature acts as an effective valley contrasting magnetic field in momentum
space[12], influencing the anomalous Hall [13] and valleyHall [14–16] effects in systems wheretime-
reversal or inversion symmetry is broken. In contrast, the BCD, which captures the asymmetric
distribution of Berry curvature, generates the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) and dominates the Hall
transport in time-reversal invariant systems with broken crystalline rotation symmetry. Together,
they offer a comprehensive framework to understand and predict the transport behavior of 2D
materials. Strain introduces an additional degree of freedom in this framework to manipulate both
BerrycurvatureandBCD.Bymodifyinglatticesymmetriesandelectronicwavefunctions,straincan
modify Berry curvature distribution in momentum space and induce asymmetries that significantly
alter the BCD [17].

Existing studies have explored how static strain affects Berry curvature and the BCD in 2D
materials. In TMDCs, strain has been shown to enhance valley-contrasting phenomena, such as
the valley Hall effect [18–20]. Moiré systems such as twisted bilayer graphene exhibit strain-tunable
Berry curvature distributions, which can modify band topology by altering Chern numbers, lead-
ing to nontrivial topological transport phenomena [21–23]. Experimental and theoretical studies
have demonstrated that strain-induced symmetry breaking enhances the BCD, giving rise to a pro-
nounced nonlinear Hall effect in materials like WTe and MoTe [24, 25]. Recent studies on twisted
doublebilayergraphene(TDBG)havedemonstratedthattheBCDcansensetopologicaltransitions
in moiré superlattices, underscoring the role of strain in tuning Berry curvature distribution and
topological properties [26, 27]. Although these findings highlight the sensitivity of Berry curvature
and BCD to strain, they predominantly address static strain, which is challenging to control due to
the inherent unpredictability of stacking-induced strain.

In this work, we introduce adiabatic oscillatory strain as a tool to dynamically modulate Berry
curvature and BCD in 2D materials, providing direct access to their temporal evolution [28, 29].
Figure 1a illustrates a representative untilted parabolic band with a symmetric Berry curvature
distribution over the Fermi surface–corresponding to a vanishing BCD. Dynamic strain perturbs
the symmetry in two distinct ways–band tilting (Figure 1b) and valley separation (Figure 1c), each
leaving a unique fingerprint in transport. The oscillatory strain periodically tilts the electronic
bands, distorting the Berry curvature distribution over the Fermi surface, leading to BCD modu-
lation as schematically shown in figure 1b. Also, the strain modulates the separation between the
K and K valleys as shown in figure 1c. Microscopically, this modifies the hopping amplitudes in
the hexagonal lattice, inducing a time-dependent gauge field [30, 31] that leads to pseudo-electric
field [32–35](See Supplementary Information section IV).

Thiscapabilityallowsforreal-timecontrolofBerrycurvatureandhelpsdisentangleothernonlin-
eareffectsfromquantumgeometriccontributions. Toexplorestrain-inducedmodulationofquantum
geometry, wefocusonTDBGandBernalBilayergraphene(BLG)fortheircomplementaryfeatures.
TDBG is a highly tunable system where the twist angle between two BLG sheets creates flat elec-
tronicbands[36,37]. Thetunabilityofitsbandstructureviaperpendicularelectricfieldandcarrier
density, combined with Berry curvature hotspots near the band edges [38–40], makes it ideal for
studying strain-driven Berry curvature dynamics. BLG, in contrast, serves as a simpler and well-
understood reference system, where a perpendicular electric field breaks inversion symmetry and
opens a bandgap at the charge neutrality point (CNP) [2]. To enable controlled strain application
in these systems, we fabricate our devices on trampoline-like, freely suspended silicon nitride mem-
branes. This platform allows mechanical coupling without substrate interference and is particularly
well suited for delicate moiré heterostructures. Through experiments on TDBG and BLG devices,
we show that strain oscillations modify the nonlinear Hall signal–arising from the time-dependent
BCD–at specific mixed frequencies, directly revealing the dynamic response of quantum geometry.
Alongside, we report direct observation of pseudo-electric field coupling to the Berry curvature,
resulting in an external field-free anomalous Hall voltage. Our findings, using versatile 2D systems,
introduce a novel approach for dynamic tuning of quantum geometric properties of materials of any
dimensionality beyond static perturbations.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal and the additional material provided, I am not convinced that the manuscript meets the conceptual novelty threshold required for publication in Nature Communications. While the responses are extensive, technically competent, and clearly written, they do not resolve the central issue: the claimed advance of “dynamic modulation of quantum geometry” does not constitute a qualitatively new physical regime, but rather a reinterpretation and repackaging of already established strain-driven transport phenomena.
The manuscript repeatedly emphasizes the term dynamic to distinguish the present work from prior studies employing surface acoustic waves (SAWs) or other time-dependent strain fields. However, from a physical standpoint, SAWs already generate explicitly time-periodic strain, leading to time-dependent band structures, gauge fields, and transport responses. Within the semiclassical Boltzmann framework used here, such time dependence necessarily implies a modulation of Berry curvature and related quantities. Consequently, the introduction of the label “dynamic quantum geometry” does not, by itself, define a new regime. The experiments are performed in the explicitly adiabatic limit (ωτ ≪ 1), where the electronic system follows the instantaneous band structure. In this limit, the response is more appropriately described as quasi-static modulation rather than genuinely dynamical quantum geometry involving non-adiabatic effects, geometric phase accumulation over a cycle, or Floquet band formation.
The authors argue that their main novelty lies in separating three contributions in the frequency domain—Berry curvature dipole modulation, coupling of a pseudo-electric field to Berry curvature, and pseudo-electric-field–band-velocity coupling. While this frequency-resolved analysis is carefully executed and pedagogically useful, it does not establish fundamentally new physics. Frequency mixing is a generic consequence of nonlinear transport under time-dependent perturbations and has already been observed and discussed extensively in SAW-based experiments. The present manuscript does not demonstrate that the observed mixed-frequency components are unique fingerprints of Berry-curvature modulation, nor that they cannot be reproduced within existing strain–gauge-field frameworks.
The comparison with Zhao et al. (PRL 128, 256601, 2022) is particularly unconvincing. The rebuttal repeatedly emphasizes that Zhao et al. studied monolayer graphene, which lacks Berry curvature at finite doping, whereas the present work focuses on TDBG and BLG. This distinction is too narrow to support a strong novelty claim. Zhao et al. already demonstrated time-dependent strain-induced synthetic electric fields, frequency-mixed Hall responses, and external-field-free transverse voltages. The present manuscript does not show that the presence of Berry curvature enables a qualitatively new observable or control mechanism; rather, it offers an alternative interpretative framework for closely related experimental signatures. Differences in terminology or band-structure context do not, on their own, constitute a Nature-level advance.
More broadly, the rebuttal relies heavily on interpretational arguments—assigning certain signals to “quantum geometry” rather than to pseudo-electromagnetic fields—without demonstrating access to a new control parameter, symmetry class, or physical limit inaccessible to prior work. A genuinely compelling case would require, for example, non-adiabatic effects, topological pumping over a strain cycle, or a geometric invariant that can only arise from time-dependent Berry curvature in a way fundamentally distinct from SAW physics.
I emphasize that this assessment does not question the technical quality of the experiments or the care with which the data are analyzed. The manuscript is well written, the measurements are competently performed, and the frequency-domain bookkeeping is clear and instructive. Nevertheless, the overall contribution represents an incremental extension and recontextualization of established strain-driven nonlinear Hall physics rather than a decisive conceptual breakthrough. For these reasons, I do not recommend publication in Nature Communications. The work would be more appropriately placed in a specialized condensed-matter journal, where its technical merits and detailed analysis can be appreciated without overstating its conceptual scope.

## Abstract

Two-dimensional materials are a fertile ground for exploring quantum geometric phenomena, with
Berry curvature and its first moment, the Berry curvature dipole, playing a central role in their
electronic response. These geometric properties influence electronic transport and result in the
anomalous and nonlinear Hall effects, and are typically controlled using static electric fields or
strain. However, the possibility of modulating quantum geometric quantities in real-time remains
unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the dynamic modulation of Berry curvature and its moments,
as well as the generation of a pseudo-electric field and their coupling. By placing heterostructures
on a membrane, we introduce oscillatory strain together with an in-plane AC electric field and
measure Hall signals that are modulated at linear combinations of the frequencies of strain and
electric field. We also present direct experimental and theoretical evidence for coupling between
pseudo-electric field and quantum geometry that results in an unusual dynamic strain-induced Hall
response. This approach opens up a new pathway for controlling quantum geometry on demand,
moving beyond conventional static perturbations. The coupling of pseudo-electric field with Berry
curvature provides a framework for external electric field-free anomalous Hall response and opens
new avenues for probing the topological properties.

## Introduction

Two-dimensional (2D) materials have emerged as an exciting platform in condensed matter physics
and material sciences, offering unique opportunities to study, tune, and probe fundamental quantum
phenomena. From graphene to transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDC) and onwards to moiré
superlattices, these atomically thin systems exhibit properties such as tunable band gaps [1, 2],
high carrier mobility, strong spin-orbit coupling [3], and pronounced excitonic effects, making them
ideal candidates for next-generation quantum devices. Among the various approaches to tailor
their properties, the application of mechanical strain stands out as a versatile and non-invasive
tool. Strain enables modification of band structures, valley polarization [4, 5], and induces phase
transitions [6, 7], thereby significantly altering the electronic and optical responses.

A particularly intriguing aspect of 2D materials is the role of quantum geometry in governing
their physical responses [8], mainly encoded by Berry curvature and the Berry curvature dipole
(BCD) [9–11]. Berry curvature acts as an effective valley contrasting magnetic field in momentum
space[12], influencing the anomalous Hall [13] and valleyHall [14–16] effects in systems wheretime-
reversal or inversion symmetry is broken. In contrast, the BCD, which captures the asymmetric
distribution of Berry curvature, generates the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) and dominates the Hall
transport in time-reversal invariant systems with broken crystalline rotation symmetry. Together,
they offer a comprehensive framework to understand and predict the transport behavior of 2D
materials. Strain introduces an additional degree of freedom in this framework to manipulate both
BerrycurvatureandBCD.Bymodifyinglatticesymmetriesandelectronicwavefunctions,straincan
modify Berry curvature distribution in momentum space and induce asymmetries that significantly
alter the BCD [17].

Existing studies have explored how static strain affects Berry curvature and the BCD in 2D
materials. In TMDCs, strain has been shown to enhance valley-contrasting phenomena, such as
the valley Hall effect [18–20]. Moiré systems such as twisted bilayer graphene exhibit strain-tunable
Berry curvature distributions, which can modify band topology by altering Chern numbers, lead-
ing to nontrivial topological transport phenomena [21–23]. Experimental and theoretical studies
have demonstrated that strain-induced symmetry breaking enhances the BCD, giving rise to a pro-

topological properties [26, 27]. Although these findings highlight the sensitivity of Berry curvature
and BCD to strain, they predominantly address static strain, which is challenging to control due to
the inherent unpredictability of stacking-induced strain.

In this work, we introduce adiabatic oscillatory strain as a tool to dynamically modulate Berry
curvature and BCD in 2D materials, providing direct access to their temporal evolution [28, 29].

### Reviewer 2

After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal and the additional material provided, I am not convinced that the manuscript meets the conceptual novelty threshold required for publication in Nature Communications. While the responses are extensive, technically competent, and clearly written, they do not resolve the central issue: the claimed advance of “dynamic modulation of quantum geometry” does not constitute a qualitatively new physical regime, but rather a reinterpretation and repackaging of already established strain-driven transport phenomena.
The manuscript repeatedly emphasizes the term dynamic to distinguish the present work from prior studies employing surface acoustic waves (SAWs) or other time-dependent strain fields. However, from a physical standpoint, SAWs already generate explicitly time-periodic strain, leading to time-dependent band structures, gauge fields, and transport responses. Within the semiclassical Boltzmann framework used here, such time dependence necessarily implies a modulation of Berry curvature and related quantities. Consequently, the introduction of the label “dynamic quantum geometry” does not, by itself, define a new regime. The experiments are performed in the explicitly adiabatic limit (ωτ ≪ 1), where the electronic system follows the instantaneous band structure. In this limit, the response is more appropriately described as quasi-static modulation rather than genuinely dynamical quantum geometry involving non-adiabatic effects, geometric phase accumulation over a cycle, or Floquet band formation.
The authors argue that their main novelty lies in separating three contributions in the frequency domain—Berry curvature dipole modulation, coupling of a pseudo-electric field to Berry curvature, and pseudo-electric-field–band-velocity coupling. While this frequency-resolved analysis is carefully executed and pedagogically useful, it does not establish fundamentally new physics. Frequency mixing is a generic consequence of nonlinear transport under time-dependent perturbations and has already been observed and discussed extensively in SAW-based experiments. The present manuscript does not demonstrate that the observed mixed-frequency components are unique fingerprints of Berry-curvature modulation, nor that they cannot be reproduced within existing strain–gauge-field frameworks.
The comparison with Zhao et al. (PRL 128, 256601, 2022) is particularly unconvincing. The rebuttal repeatedly emphasizes that Zhao et al. studied monolayer graphene, which lacks Berry curvature at finite doping, whereas the present work focuses on TDBG and BLG. This distinction is too narrow to support a strong novelty claim. Zhao et al. already demonstrated time-dependent strain-induced synthetic electric fields, frequency-mixed Hall responses, and external-field-free transverse voltages. The present manuscript does not show that the presence of Berry curvature enables a qualitatively new observable or control mechanism; rather, it offers an alternative interpretative framework for closely related experimental signatures. Differences in terminology or band-structure context do not, on their own, constitute a Nature-level advance.
More broadly, the rebuttal relies heavily on interpretational arguments—assigning certain signals to “quantum geometry” rather than to pseudo-electromagnetic fields—without demonstrating access to a new control parameter, symmetry class, or physical limit inaccessible to prior work. Interpretation alone, however elegant, is insufficient justification for publication in Nature Communications. A genuinely compelling case would require, for example, non-adiabatic effects, topological pumping over a strain cycle, or a geometric invariant that can only arise from time-dependent Berry curvature in a way fundamentally distinct from SAW physics.
I emphasize that this assessment does not question the technical quality of the experiments or the care with which the data are analyzed. The manuscript is well written, the measurements are competently performed, and the frequency-domain bookkeeping is clear and instructive. Nevertheless, the overall contribution represents an incremental extension and recontextualization of established strain-driven nonlinear Hall physics rather than a decisive conceptual breakthrough. For these reasons, I do not recommend publication in Nature Communications. The work would be more appropriately placed in a specialized condensed-matter journal, where its technical merits and detailed analysis can be appreciated without overstating its conceptual scope.

### Reviewer 3

The revised manuscript by S. Layek et al. has thoughtfully addressed all issues raised by three reviewers. The updated manuscript and supplementary information included new illustrations and experimental results that better clarified several key points. This manuscript is now well written, which contains convincing experimental and theoretical evidence that demonstrates unusual dynamic strain-induced Hall response due to coupling between pseudo-electric field and quantum geometry in twisted double bilayer graphene (TDBG) with two different twist angles and in Bernal bilayer graphene (BLG). Additionally, the underlying concepts have the potential of being generalized to systems of any dimensionality if they possess Berry curvature. Therefore, the revised manuscript is now suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
